summary: How blood cells look on a smear, where they come from, and how they mature. Exam questions ask you to name a cell from its nucleus and granules, trace a lineage back to its progenitor, read a left shift or a high reticulocyte count, and explain why marrow failure or ineffective erythropoiesis enlarges the spleen.

points: Red cell: about 7 to 8 µm, no nucleus, pink biconcave disc with central pallor about one third of its width.
Segmented neutrophil: 3 to 5 lobes joined by thin strands, fine pale pink to lilac granules.
Band: curved, horseshoe-shaped nucleus with no true segments; an immature neutrophil.
Eosinophil: usually two lobes, large bright orange-red granules.
Basophil: dark blue-purple granules that hide the nucleus; the rarest white cell.
Small lymphocyte: about the size of a red cell, round dark nucleus, thin rim of pale blue cytoplasm.
Monocyte: the largest white cell, folded or kidney-shaped nucleus, gray-blue cytoplasm, sometimes vacuoles.
Platelets: small (about 2 to 3 µm) purple-granular fragments with no nucleus.
notes.why: Wright stain pairs eosin, an acidic dye that colors basic proteins such as hemoglobin and eosinophil major basic protein orange-pink, with methylene blue derivatives, basic dyes that color acidic material such as DNA, RNA, and the sulfated proteoglycans of basophil granules blue to purple. Cytoplasm color tracks ribosome content, so RNA-rich lymphocyte and monocyte cytoplasm looks blue while a mature red cell full of hemoglobin looks pink. In the granulocyte line, nuclear shape tracks maturity, so a segmented nucleus marks a mature neutrophil and a horseshoe nucleus marks a band.

points: The hematopoietic stem cell (CD34 positive) self-renews and gives two progenitors: common myeloid and common lymphoid.
Common myeloid progenitor: red cells, megakaryocytes (platelets), neutrophils, monocytes (which become tissue macrophages), eosinophils, basophils, and mast cells.
Common lymphoid progenitor: B cells, T cells (finish maturing in the thymus), and NK cells.
notes.why: Each branch point commits a progenitor to one fate through lineage-specific transcription factors and growth factor receptors, and the cell loses the ability to make other lineages. The early split into common myeloid and common lymphoid progenitors explains why a myeloproliferative neoplasm, which arises in a stem or early myeloid cell, often raises red cells, granulocytes, and platelets together. Final maturation can happen outside the marrow: monocytes become macrophages in tissues, and T cell precursors finish selection in the thymus.

points: Yolk sac blood islands from about week 3, then the liver (main fetal site from about week 6), with a smaller contribution from the spleen.
Bone marrow takes over in the second half of gestation and is the main site at birth.
In adults, active red marrow sits mainly in the axial skeleton (vertebrae, sternum, ribs, pelvis, skull) and proximal femur and humerus.
Extramedullary hematopoiesis returns to the liver and spleen when the marrow fails or cannot keep up, causing hepatosplenomegaly.
Myelofibrosis: fibrotic marrow, massive splenomegaly, teardrop cells, and a leukoerythroblastic smear (nucleated red cells plus immature granulocytes).
Beta thalassemia major: ineffective erythropoiesis expands the marrow (crew-cut skull, prominent cheekbones) and drives splenic and hepatic blood formation.
notes.why: Blood forms wherever there is a supportive niche of stromal cells and growth factors: first the yolk sac, then the fetal liver, then bone marrow once bones develop marrow cavities. The liver and spleen keep the ability to support hematopoiesis after birth, so stem cells resettle there when the marrow is scarred or cannot meet demand. In myelofibrosis, cells released from the distorted marrow and from extramedullary sites give teardrop cells and a leukoerythroblastic smear, while in beta thalassemia major intense but ineffective erythropoiesis expands both the marrow space and extramedullary sites, enlarging the liver and spleen.

points: Proerythroblast, basophilic erythroblast, polychromatophilic erythroblast, orthochromatic erythroblast, reticulocyte, mature red cell.
Along the way the cell shrinks, the nucleus condenses and is extruded, and hemoglobin builds up, so cytoplasm turns from blue (ribosomes) to pink (hemoglobin).
The reticulocyte has no nucleus but keeps ribosomal RNA, which shows as a blue-gray tint on Wright stain and a reticular network with supravital stains.
Reticulocytes lose their RNA in about one day in the blood; the normal count is about 0.5 to 1.5%.
A high reticulocyte count means the marrow is answering anemia (hemolysis or blood loss); a low count with anemia means underproduction.
notes.why: Erythroid maturation builds hemoglobin while dismantling everything else. Early erythroblasts are packed with ribosomes making globin, which makes the cytoplasm blue, and as hemoglobin accumulates and ribosomes decline the cytoplasm passes through a gray (polychromatophilic) stage to pink. The condensed nucleus is extruded and the reticulocyte keeps residual ribosomal RNA for only about a day in the blood, so the reticulocyte count is a direct readout of recent marrow output. A high count in anemia shows a working marrow and points to blood loss or destruction.

points: Myeloblast, promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band, segmented neutrophil.
Promyelocytes make the primary (azurophilic) granules with myeloperoxidase; specific granules appear at the myelocyte stage.
The myelocyte is the last stage that can divide; from the metamyelocyte on, cells only mature.
Left shift: more bands and earlier forms (metamyelocytes, myelocytes) in the blood, as in acute bacterial infection.
notes.why: Granule types are made at set stages, so granule content dates the cell: azurophilic granules with myeloperoxidase are made at the promyelocyte stage and specific granules begin at the myelocyte stage. After the myelocyte stage cells stop dividing and only mature, so the marrow holds a large storage pool of metamyelocytes, bands, and segmented neutrophils. In acute bacterial infection, cytokines such as G-CSF and IL-1 release this pool faster than it can mature, so bands and earlier forms appear in the blood as a left shift.

points: Megakaryocytes are huge polyploid marrow cells (endomitosis) that push cytoplasmic extensions into sinusoids and shed platelets.
Alpha granules: von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, fibronectin, platelet factor 4, and PDGF.
Dense (delta) granules: ADP, calcium, and serotonin.
notes.why: Megakaryocytes replicate their DNA without dividing (endomitosis), which builds a large polyploid cell with enough cytoplasm to shed thousands of platelets into the marrow sinusoids. Platelets have no nucleus, so their granules are preloaded tools for hemostasis. Alpha granule von Willebrand factor and fibrinogen support adhesion and aggregation, dense granule ADP and serotonin recruit more platelets and constrict the vessel, and calcium supports the coagulation reactions that assemble on the platelet surface.

notes.h: B and T zones in lymph node and spleen
points: Lymph node cortex: follicles of B cells; germinal centers form in secondary follicles after antigen exposure.
Lymph node paracortex: T cells and high endothelial venules where lymphocytes enter from blood.
Lymph node medulla: medullary cords (plasma cells, macrophages) and medullary sinuses that drain to the efferent lymphatic.
Spleen white pulp: periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (T cells) around central arterioles and follicles (B cells).
Spleen marginal zone: between white and red pulp; macrophages and marginal zone B cells trap blood-borne antigens.
Spleen red pulp: cords of Billroth and sinusoids; red cells must squeeze through slits in sinusoid walls, and old or rigid cells are removed.
notes.why: In the lymph node, dendritic cells carry antigen from afferent lymph into the paracortex, where T cells entering through high endothelial venules screen it, and activated helper T cells then help B cells at the follicle edge, driving germinal centers and plasma cells that settle in the medullary cords. The spleen samples blood instead of lymph, so its marginal zone traps blood-borne antigens and its red pulp tests red cell deformability at slits in the sinusoid walls. This layout explains why T cell deficiency depletes the paracortex and PALS, while B cell deficiency leaves nodes without follicles or germinal centers.

summary: What blood is made of and what each part does: plasma proteins, red cell design for gas transport, erythropoietin control, white cell jobs, and ABO and Rh typing. Exam questions ask you to read a CBC to classify an anemia, predict erythropoietin in different settings, explain edema from low albumin, and pick a safe donor.

points: Plasma is about 55% of blood volume and is about 92% water, with proteins, electrolytes, nutrients, hormones, gases, and wastes.
Plasma proteins: albumin (about 55 to 60%), globulins (about 35%, including immunoglobulins and transport proteins), and fibrinogen (about 4%).
Serum is the fluid left after blood clots, so it lacks fibrinogen and the clotting factors used up in clotting.
Plasma comes from blood drawn into an anticoagulant tube (citrate, EDTA, or heparin).
notes.why: Plasma is the fluid phase of unclotted blood, so it keeps fibrinogen and every clotting factor; anticoagulant tubes work by chelating calcium (citrate, EDTA) or by boosting antithrombin (heparin). When blood clots, fibrinogen becomes fibrin and factors such as V and VIII are consumed, so serum is plasma minus those proteins. This is why PT and PTT are run on citrated plasma, while serum protein electrophoresis uses serum so that fibrinogen does not appear as an extra band.

points: Made by the liver; provides most (about 75 to 80%) of plasma oncotic pressure.
Carries unconjugated bilirubin, free fatty acids, calcium (most of the protein-bound calcium, which is about 40% of the total), hormones, and many drugs.
Starling forces: capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out; plasma oncotic pressure pulls it back.
Low albumin (nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, protein malnutrition) lowers capillary oncotic pressure, so net filtration rises and edema forms.
Low albumin lowers total calcium while ionized calcium stays normal.
notes.why: Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein and does not cross the capillary wall easily, so it supplies most of the plasma oncotic pressure. In Starling terms, net filtration is the hydrostatic gradient out of the capillary minus the oncotic gradient pulling fluid back in, so a low albumin weakens the inward force and fluid collects in the interstitium once filtration outpaces lymph flow. Albumin also binds unconjugated bilirubin, fatty acids, and calcium, so hypoalbuminemia lowers total calcium while the physiologically active ionized calcium stays normal.

notes.h: Red cell design for gas transport
points: Biconcave shape gives a large surface area for diffusion and lets the cell fold through capillaries and splenic slits.
No nucleus or organelles leaves more room for hemoglobin; no mitochondria means the cell does not use the oxygen it carries and makes ATP by glycolysis.
Carbonic anhydrase in red cells turns CO2 and water into carbonic acid, which splits into H+ and bicarbonate.
Most CO2 (about 70%) travels in plasma as bicarbonate; H+ is buffered by deoxyhemoglobin.
Chloride shift: bicarbonate leaves the red cell through band 3 in exchange for chloride, and the process reverses in the lungs.
notes.why: Losing the nucleus and organelles leaves room for hemoglobin, and without mitochondria the cell makes ATP by glycolysis and uses none of the oxygen it carries. The biconcave disc has extra membrane for its volume, which shortens diffusion distance and lets the cell fold through capillaries and splenic slits. Carbonic anhydrase converts CO2 to bicarbonate within the cell, band 3 exports the bicarbonate in exchange for chloride, and deoxyhemoglobin buffers the H+, so releasing O2 in tissues helps the blood take up CO2 (the Haldane effect).

points: Made mainly by peritubular interstitial (fibroblast-like) cells of the renal cortex, with a small amount from the liver.
Low tissue oxygen stabilizes hypoxia-inducible factor, which turns on the erythropoietin gene.
Erythropoietin keeps erythroid progenitors alive and speeds their maturation, so reticulocytes rise within days.
Erythropoietin tracks oxygen delivery to the kidney, so it rises with hypoxemia or anemia and falls when red cell mass is high.
notes.why: In normal oxygen, prolyl hydroxylases use O2 to mark hypoxia-inducible factor alpha (HIF-alpha) for destruction by the von Hippel-Lindau protein; in hypoxia HIF-alpha escapes degradation and switches on the erythropoietin gene in renal peritubular interstitial cells. Erythropoietin keeps late erythroid progenitors and early erythroblasts from undergoing apoptosis, so red cell output rises over several days. This predicts low erythropoietin in chronic kidney disease (loss of producing cells), high levels at altitude, and suppressed levels in polycythemia vera, where mutant JAK2 drives red cell production without the hormone.

points: Reference values: hemoglobin about 13.5 to 17.5 g/dL in men and 12 to 16 g/dL in women; hematocrit about 41 to 53% in men and 36 to 46% in women; MCV 80 to 100 fL; MCHC 32 to 36 g/dL; RDW about 11.5 to 14.5%.
MCV sorts the anemia: under 80 fL microcytic, 80 to 100 fL normocytic, over 100 fL macrocytic.
Microcytic: iron deficiency, thalassemia, anemia of chronic disease (some cases), sideroblastic anemia including lead poisoning.
Macrocytic: megaloblastic (B12 or folate deficiency) or nonmegaloblastic (alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, marked reticulocytosis).
Reticulocyte count separates hemolysis or blood loss (high) from underproduction (low or normal).
High RDW means mixed cell sizes, as in iron deficiency; RDW is usually normal in thalassemia trait.
High MCHC is a clue to hereditary spherocytosis.
notes.why: The indices describe the average red cell, and each pattern points to a step in production. Microcytosis means hemoglobin synthesis failed (too little iron, heme, or globin), so cells come out small and pale, while megaloblastic macrocytosis means DNA synthesis lagged behind cytoplasmic growth. The reticulocyte count then asks whether the marrow is responding: high with hemolysis or bleeding, low when the marrow cannot produce. RDW measures variation in size, so it rises in iron deficiency as new small cells mix with older normal ones, and stays normal in thalassemia trait, where every cell is uniformly small.

points: Neutrophils: phagocytose and kill bacteria with the respiratory burst; neutrophilia means bacterial infection (also steroids and stress).
Eosinophils: attack helminths with major basic protein and modulate allergic reactions; eosinophilia means parasites or allergy.
Basophils: release histamine and heparin; basophilia is a clue to myeloproliferative disease such as CML.
Monocytes: become tissue macrophages and present antigen; monocytosis appears in chronic infection such as tuberculosis.
Lymphocytes: B cells make antibody, T cells direct and kill, NK cells kill infected cells; lymphocytosis means viral infection (also pertussis and CLL).
notes.why: Each white cell's granules and receptors match the threat it handles. Neutrophils kill ingested bacteria with NADPH oxidase, which makes superoxide, and myeloperoxidase, which turns hydrogen peroxide into hypochlorous acid, so bacterial infection mobilizes them from marrow stores. Eosinophils are recruited by IL-5 from Th2 cells and degranulate onto helminths too large to engulf, which is why parasites and allergy share eosinophilia. Viral infection drives lymphocytosis because killing infected host cells is the job of cytotoxic T cells and NK cells.

points: A and B antigens are sugars added to the H antigen on red cells; type O has unmodified H antigen.
People make IgM anti-A and anti-B against the antigens they lack, starting in the first months of life after exposure to similar gut bacterial sugars.
Red cell transfusion: donor cells must lack antigens the recipient has antibodies against. O cells go to anyone; AB recipients take any ABO type.
Plasma transfusion runs the other way: AB plasma has no anti-A or anti-B and is the universal plasma donor.
Rh (D antigen): Rh-negative people make anti-D only after exposure (transfusion or pregnancy), and it is IgG that crosses the placenta.
notes.why: Glycosyltransferases encoded at the ABO locus add N-acetylgalactosamine (A) or galactose (B) to the H antigen, and type O lacks a working transferase, so it keeps unmodified H. Gut bacteria carry similar sugars, so infants make IgM anti-A and anti-B against whichever antigens they lack without any transfusion. These IgM antibodies fix complement strongly, which is why an ABO-mismatched red cell transfusion causes immediate intravascular hemolysis. RhD is a protein antigen with no common environmental look-alike, so anti-D forms only after exposure and is IgG, which crosses the placenta.

tricks.text: First, what is the MCV (small, normal, large)? Second, is the reticulocyte count high (hemolysis or bleeding) or low (production problem)? Most anemias fall out of those two answers.

highYield: Edema with albumin of 2.0 g/dL (reference 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL) comes from low plasma oncotic pressure.
Polycythemia vera has low erythropoietin; secondary polycythemia from hypoxia or an erythropoietin-secreting tumor has high erythropoietin.
Normocytic anemia with a low reticulocyte count in chronic kidney disease reflects loss of erythropoietin production.
Microcytosis with a high RDW suggests iron deficiency; microcytosis with a normal RDW and a normal or high red cell count suggests thalassemia trait.
Venous red cells contain more chloride than arterial red cells because of the chloride shift.
Type O, Rh-negative red cells are given when there is no time to type the patient.
Lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes suggests a viral infection such as infectious mononucleosis.
pitfalls: Serum and plasma are swapped often: serum has no fibrinogen because it has clotted.
Universal donor rules flip between red cells (O) and plasma (AB).
Anti-A and anti-B are naturally occurring IgM, while anti-D appears only after exposure and is IgG.
A low total calcium with low albumin does not mean true hypocalcemia if ionized calcium is normal.
Erythropoietin is made by renal interstitial cells, and juxtaglomerular cells make renin.

summary: How blood cells are removed and their parts recycled: red cell life span, heme breakdown to bilirubin, iron handling, and the two patterns of hemolysis. Exam questions ask you to trace bilirubin, read haptoglobin and urine findings to place hemolysis inside or outside vessels, interpret hepcidin and iron studies, and predict which cell count falls first when the marrow stops.

notes.h: Red cell life span and removal
points: Red cells live about 120 days; with no nucleus they cannot repair membrane or enzyme damage.
Aging cells grow stiff and are removed mainly by macrophages of the splenic red pulp, with help from liver and marrow macrophages.
Globin is broken into amino acids, iron is recycled, and heme is turned into bilirubin.
notes.why: Without a nucleus or ribosomes the red cell cannot replace damaged membrane proteins or enzymes, so over about 120 days it stiffens and displays signs of age such as exposed phosphatidylserine and clustered band 3. The splenic red pulp is the test: cells must squeeze through slits between sinusoid endothelial cells, and stiff cells held back in the cords are eaten by macrophages. Inside the macrophage, globin is broken into amino acids, iron is returned to plasma transferrin through ferroportin, and the heme ring is degraded to bilirubin.

points: Heme oxygenase in macrophages opens the heme ring, releasing iron and carbon monoxide and forming green biliverdin.
Biliverdin reductase makes unconjugated bilirubin, which is fat soluble, water insoluble, and toxic to the brain in newborns.
Unconjugated bilirubin travels bound to albumin, so it does not pass into urine.
Hepatocytes take it up and conjugate it with glucuronic acid using UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1).
Conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and is secreted into bile.
Gut bacteria turn it into urobilinogen; most becomes stercobilin (brown stool color), some is reabsorbed, and a little leaves in urine as yellow urobilin.
Hemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin and urine urobilinogen with no bilirubin in urine, and chronic hemolysis causes black pigment gallstones.
notes.why: Bilirubin's water solubility decides where it can go. Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid soluble, so it travels bound to albumin, is not filtered into urine, and in newborns the free fraction can cross the blood-brain barrier (kernicterus). Conjugation with glucuronic acid by UGT1A1 makes it water soluble for secretion into bile, and gut bacteria then reduce it to urobilinogen, part of which is reabsorbed and excreted in urine as urobilin. In hemolysis, bilirubin production outpaces hepatic uptake and conjugation, so unconjugated bilirubin and urine urobilinogen rise while urine bilirubin stays negative.

points: Extravascular: macrophages in the spleen and liver eat damaged or antibody-coated cells; spherocytes and splenomegaly are typical.
Intravascular: cells burst inside vessels, releasing free hemoglobin into plasma.
Free hemoglobin binds haptoglobin, so haptoglobin becomes very low or undetectable.
Once haptoglobin is saturated, hemoglobin passes into urine (hemoglobinuria, dark urine).
Kidney tubular cells take up the filtered hemoglobin and later shed iron-laden cells, giving hemosiderinuria days later.
Both types raise LDH, unconjugated bilirubin, and the reticulocyte count.
notes.why: Where the red cell is destroyed decides which markers change. In extravascular hemolysis macrophages digest the cell and process the heme internally, so little free hemoglobin reaches plasma; partial removal of antibody-coated membrane leaves spherocytes, and the hard-working spleen enlarges. In intravascular hemolysis, haptoglobin binds the free hemoglobin and the complex is cleared by macrophages, mainly in the liver, so haptoglobin is used up; after that, hemoglobin dimers pass the glomerulus, appear as hemoglobinuria, and are absorbed by proximal tubule cells that shed hemosiderin days later. LDH and unconjugated bilirubin rise in both because both release red cell contents and add heme for degradation.

points: Duodenal cytochrome b reduces dietary ferric iron (Fe3+) to ferrous iron (Fe2+), and DMT1 carries it into the duodenal enterocyte.
Heme iron from meat is absorbed by a separate route and more efficiently.
Iron leaves the enterocyte (and macrophages) through ferroportin; hephaestin reoxidizes it to Fe3+ for transport.
Transferrin carries iron in plasma to marrow, where cells take it in through transferrin receptors.
Ferritin stores iron inside cells (liver, macrophages); serum ferritin reflects stores but also rises with inflammation.
Hepcidin from the liver binds ferroportin and causes its breakdown, blocking both gut absorption and macrophage release.
Hepcidin rises with inflammation (IL-6) and iron excess, and falls with iron deficiency, hypoxia, and active erythropoiesis.
The body has no regulated route to excrete iron, so absorption is the control point.
notes.why: Iron is essential but toxic, and the body has no regulated way to excrete it, so control happens where iron enters plasma. Ferroportin is the only known cellular iron exporter, used by duodenal enterocytes, macrophages recycling old red cells, and hepatocytes, and hepcidin binds ferroportin and triggers its internalization and breakdown. High hepcidin traps iron inside enterocytes (lost when they are shed) and macrophages, which explains the low serum iron with normal or high ferritin of anemia of chronic disease, where IL-6 raises hepcidin. Low hepcidin in iron deficiency or active erythropoiesis lets ferroportin export freely, and inappropriately low hepcidin is the basis of hereditary hemochromatosis.

points: Neutrophils circulate only about 6 to 8 hours, platelets about 7 to 10 days, and red cells about 120 days.
After sudden marrow suppression (chemotherapy, radiation, drug-induced aplasia), neutrophils fall first, platelets next, and anemia appears last.
Neutropenia brings infection risk within about 1 to 2 weeks, while hemoglobin drops slowly over weeks.
notes.why: After sudden marrow injury, existing cells keep circulating until they age out while no replacements arrive, so counts fall in order of circulating life span. Neutrophils last hours in blood and the marrow storage pool lasts only days, so neutropenia appears first; platelets last 7 to 10 days, so thrombocytopenia follows. Red cells last about 120 days, so red cell mass falls by only about 1% a day without production, which is why a patient after chemotherapy presents with fever from neutropenia or bleeding well before significant anemia.

tricks.label: Haptoglobin is the mop
tricks.text: Haptoglobin mops up free hemoglobin in plasma. When cells burst inside vessels the mop is used up, so very low haptoglobin plus hemoglobinuria points to intravascular hemolysis.

tricks.label: Hepcidin locks the door
tricks.text: Ferroportin is the only exit door for iron from gut cells and macrophages. Hepcidin locks it, so high hepcidin traps iron in macrophages (anemia of chronic disease) and low hepcidin leaves the door open (hemochromatosis).

tricks.label: Short life, first to fall
tricks.text: Order the counts by life span: neutrophils (hours), platelets (days), red cells (months). The shorter the life, the sooner the count falls when production stops.

summary: How blood cell production is driven by growth factors and how bleeding is stopped and then limited. Exam questions ask you to walk through platelet plug formation and the clotting cascade, match PT and PTT to their pathways, use a mixing study to find an inhibitor, and apply Virchow triad to a patient with a clot.

points: Erythropoietin (kidney): red cells.
Thrombopoietin (made mostly in the liver): megakaryocytes and platelets.
G-CSF: neutrophils; GM-CSF: granulocytes and monocytes.
IL-5 (from Th2 cells): eosinophils.
IL-3 and stem cell factor (kit ligand) act on early multipotent progenitors.
notes.why: Each growth factor acts on the progenitors that carry its receptor, and most of these receptors signal through JAK-STAT to block apoptosis and drive proliferation and maturation. Early multipotent progenitors respond to stem cell factor and IL-3, while committed progenitors depend on one dominant factor, so erythropoietin, thrombopoietin, G-CSF, and IL-5 can each raise a single cell line. Thrombopoietin is made at a fairly steady rate by the liver and removed by binding to receptors on platelets and megakaryocytes, so free levels rise when platelets are few and fall when they are plentiful.

points: Injury causes brief reflex vasoconstriction, helped by endothelin.
Adhesion: von Willebrand factor binds exposed subendothelial collagen and the platelet receptor GpIb.
Activation: platelets change shape and degranulate, releasing ADP from dense granules and making thromboxane A2 through COX-1.
ADP (via P2Y12) and thromboxane A2 recruit more platelets and switch on GpIIb/IIIa.
Aggregation: fibrinogen links GpIIb/IIIa receptors on neighboring platelets into a plug.
Platelet defects show as mucosal bleeding and petechiae with a prolonged bleeding time.
notes.why: Under the high shear of arterial flow, platelets can stop only because von Willebrand factor unfolds on exposed collagen and grabs platelet GpIb, slowing them enough to attach. Adhesion activates the platelet, which releases ADP and makes thromboxane A2 by COX-1; both act on nearby platelets and switch GpIIb/IIIa into its high-affinity form. Fibrinogen is a symmetric molecule that can bind GpIIb/IIIa on two platelets at once, so it bridges them into a plug. This sequence explains why aspirin, P2Y12 blockers, von Willebrand disease, Bernard-Soulier syndrome (GpIb), and Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GpIIb/IIIa) cause mucosal bleeding with a normal PT.

points: Extrinsic (tissue factor) pathway: tissue factor exposed at injury binds factor VIIa and activates factors X and IX; this starts clotting in the body.
Intrinsic (contact) pathway: XII, XI, IX, and VIII; IXa with VIIIa activates X.
Common pathway: Xa with Va, on phospholipid with calcium, converts prothrombin (II) to thrombin.
Thrombin cleaves fibrinogen to fibrin and also activates V, VIII, XI, XIII, and platelets, amplifying itself.
Factor XIIIa cross-links fibrin, making the clot stable.
PT measures extrinsic and common pathways (VII, X, V, II, fibrinogen); INR standardizes PT for warfarin monitoring.
PTT measures intrinsic and common pathways (XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, fibrinogen); it monitors unfractionated heparin.
notes.why: In the body, tissue factor at the injury binds factor VIIa and produces a small amount of thrombin, which then activates factors V, VIII, and XI and platelets. The IXa with VIIIa complex and the Xa with Va complex then assemble on the activated platelet surface and amplify thrombin generation many times over. Factor XII is not needed for normal hemostasis, so its deficiency prolongs the PTT without bleeding. The tests split the system artificially: PT starts clotting with tissue factor and detects deficits in VII and the common pathway, while PTT starts with a contact activator and detects deficits in XII, XI, IX, VIII, and the common pathway.

points: Antithrombin inactivates thrombin and factor Xa (and IXa, XIa, XIIa); heparin speeds this greatly.
Thrombomodulin on endothelium binds thrombin, which then activates protein C.
Activated protein C, with protein S as cofactor, cleaves and inactivates factors Va and VIIIa.
Tissue factor pathway inhibitor blocks the tissue factor and VIIa complex once Xa forms.
tPA from endothelium converts plasminogen to plasmin on the fibrin surface.
Plasmin breaks fibrin and fibrinogen into fibrin degradation products; D-dimer comes only from cross-linked fibrin, so it shows a clot formed and is being broken down.
notes.why: Healthy endothelium around an injury actively switches clotting off so the clot stays local. Antithrombin has low activity until heparin or endothelial heparan sulfate changes its shape, after which it rapidly inactivates thrombin and factor Xa. Thrombin bound to thrombomodulin stops cleaving fibrinogen and instead activates protein C, which with protein S cleaves factors Va and VIIIa, removing the cofactors that drive the amplifying complexes. Fibrin binds both tPA and plasminogen, so plasmin forms right on the clot, and D-dimer appears only when plasmin digests fibrin that factor XIIIa has cross-linked.

points: Patient plasma is mixed 1:1 with normal plasma and the prolonged test is repeated.
If the time corrects, a factor is missing (normal plasma supplies enough).
If it does not correct, an inhibitor is present, such as an acquired factor VIII antibody, lupus anticoagulant, or heparin.
notes.why: A clotting time is prolonged either because a factor is low or because something blocks a factor or the reaction. Mixing with an equal volume of normal plasma brings any deficient factor to about 50% of normal, which is enough to normalize the PT or PTT, so correction points to a deficiency. An inhibitor acts on the factors in the added normal plasma as well, so the time stays long; acquired factor VIII inhibitors are time and temperature dependent, so the mix may correct at first and prolong again after incubation at 37 °C (98.6 °F).

points: Stasis: immobility, long travel, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, pregnant uterus compressing pelvic veins.
Endothelial injury: surgery (especially hip and knee), trauma, central venous catheters.
Hypercoagulability: pregnancy and estrogen (more clotting factors, less protein S), malignancy (tumor tissue factor and mucin), inherited thrombophilia.
Surgery adds all three: vessel injury, bed rest, and tissue factor release.
notes.why: Venous thrombi form in slow flow, where activated factors are not washed away and the endothelium of valve pockets becomes hypoxic, which is why stasis dominates venous thrombosis and endothelial injury dominates arterial thrombosis. Hypercoagulable states tip the balance between procoagulant and anticoagulant proteins: estrogen raises hepatic synthesis of several clotting factors and lowers protein S, and tumors express tissue factor and release procoagulant mucins. Major orthopedic surgery adds all three arms at once, which explains its high risk and the routine use of prophylaxis.

summary: The biochemistry behind red cells and clotting: heme synthesis and the porphyrias, hemoglobin oxygen binding, methemoglobin and carbon monoxide, red cell energy and antioxidant pathways, B12 and folate, and vitamin K. Exam questions ask you to place a block in a pathway, predict which way the oxygen curve shifts, and use lab markers to name the missing vitamin or enzyme.

points: Starts in the mitochondrion: glycine plus succinyl-CoA form delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) by ALA synthase, the rate-limiting enzyme, which needs pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6).
Heme represses ALA synthase (feedback), and drugs that increase cytochrome P450 demand for heme induce it.

Cytosol: ALA dehydratase joins two ALA into porphobilinogen; porphobilinogen deaminase builds hydroxymethylbilane, which becomes uroporphyrinogen III; uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase converts that to coproporphyrinogen III.
Back in the mitochondrion: protoporphyrin IX is formed and ferrochelatase inserts ferrous iron to make heme.
Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, causing microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling and raised protoporphyrin.
B6 deficiency (for example with isoniazid) lowers ALA synthase activity and causes sideroblastic anemia.
notes.why: The pathway begins and ends in the mitochondrion because succinyl-CoA comes from the citric acid cycle and ferrochelatase sits on the inner mitochondrial membrane, while the middle steps run in the cytosol. ALA synthase sets the rate and free heme represses the hepatic form, so drugs that use up heme by inducing cytochrome P450 enzymes raise ALA synthase activity. ALA synthase needs pyridoxal phosphate, so B6 deficiency starves the pathway at its first step and unused iron collects in mitochondria around the nucleus as ringed sideroblasts. Lead blocks ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, so ALA and protoporphyrin accumulate while heme output falls.

points: Acute intermittent porphyria: porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency (autosomal dominant); ALA and porphobilinogen build up.
Acute attacks: severe abdominal pain, neuropathy, psychiatric symptoms, and urine that darkens on standing; no skin photosensitivity.
Attacks are triggered by anything that induces ALA synthase: P450-inducing drugs, alcohol, fasting, and hormonal changes.
Porphyria cutanea tarda: uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency, the most common porphyria; uroporphyrin builds up.
PCT findings: blistering and fragile skin on sun-exposed areas (backs of hands), hypertrichosis, and tea-colored urine; linked to hepatitis C, alcohol, and iron overload.
notes.why: Each porphyria is defined by the intermediate that builds up behind the blocked enzyme, and the chemistry of that intermediate sets the symptoms. Early precursors (ALA and porphobilinogen) do not absorb light but are thought to be neurotoxic, so acute intermittent porphyria causes visceral pain, neuropathy, and psychiatric symptoms without skin findings. Later intermediates oxidize to ring-shaped porphyrins that absorb light and generate reactive oxygen species in the skin, so porphyria cutanea tarda causes blistering of sun-exposed skin. AIP attacks follow anything that induces hepatic ALA synthase, while PCT appears when iron overload, alcohol, or hepatitis C further suppress an already reduced uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase.

points: HbA is two alpha and two beta chains (about 95 to 97% of adult hemoglobin); HbA2 is two alpha and two delta (about 2 to 3%); HbF is two alpha and two gamma (main fetal form, under 1% in adults).
Binding is cooperative: each O2 bound shifts hemoglobin from the low-affinity taut state toward the high-affinity relaxed state, giving a sigmoid curve.
Right shift (lower affinity, more O2 unloaded): higher 2,3-BPG, H+ (lower pH), CO2, and temperature, as in exercising muscle.
Left shift (higher affinity, less unloaded): HbF (binds 2,3-BPG poorly), carbon monoxide, methemoglobin, alkalosis, cold, and low 2,3-BPG.
notes.why: Binding one O2 shifts hemoglobin from the tense (T) toward the relaxed (R) state, so the next O2 binds more easily, giving a sigmoid curve that loads fully in the lungs and unloads steeply in tissues. Anything that stabilizes the T state, such as 2,3-BPG in the central cavity between the beta chains, H+ and CO2 (the Bohr effect), and heat, shifts the curve right and favors unloading in active tissue. HbF has gamma chains that bind 2,3-BPG weakly, so its higher affinity pulls O2 across the placenta from maternal HbA. Carbon monoxide and methemoglobin shift the curve left by holding the remaining sites in a high-affinity state.

points: Methemoglobin has ferric iron (Fe3+), which cannot carry O2 and left-shifts the remaining sites, so delivery falls while PaO2 stays normal.
Clues: cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen, chocolate-brown blood, and pulse oximetry stuck around 85%.
NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase normally keeps iron ferrous; congenital deficiency of this enzyme causes lifelong methemoglobinemia.
Acquired causes: nitrites, dapsone, benzocaine and other topical anesthetics.
Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin about 200 times more tightly than O2, lowering O2 content and left-shifting the curve with a normal PaO2.
notes.why: PaO2 measures oxygen dissolved in plasma, so it stays normal when hemoglobin itself is disabled. Methemoglobin's ferric iron cannot bind O2 and carbon monoxide occupies binding sites with far higher affinity, so both lower oxygen content, and by left-shifting the remaining sites they also hinder unloading of the oxygen that is carried. NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase normally reduces the small amount of methemoglobin formed each day, so a congenital deficiency or an oxidant drug that outpaces it causes cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen. Standard pulse oximetry reads carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin and drifts toward about 85% with methemoglobin, so saturation alone misses both.

notes.h: Red cell energy and antioxidant defense
points: With no mitochondria, red cells get all ATP from glycolysis; ATP runs Na+/K+-ATPase and keeps the membrane flexible.
Pyruvate kinase deficiency: low ATP, rigid cells, extravascular hemolysis; 2,3-BPG builds up upstream and right-shifts the curve.
The pentose phosphate pathway (G6PD step) is the red cell's only NADPH source.
NADPH keeps glutathione reduced, and reduced glutathione clears hydrogen peroxide.
G6PD deficiency: oxidant stress (infection, fava beans, sulfonamides, primaquine, dapsone) denatures hemoglobin into Heinz bodies; splenic macrophages bite them out, leaving bite cells.
notes.why: Mature red cells have no mitochondria, so glycolysis is their only ATP source and the pentose phosphate pathway is their only NADPH source. ATP powers ion pumps and membrane upkeep; in pyruvate kinase deficiency ATP falls, cells lose potassium and water, stiffen, and are removed by the spleen, while upstream intermediates including 2,3-BPG build up and right-shift the curve. NADPH from the G6PD step keeps glutathione reduced so glutathione peroxidase can clear hydrogen peroxide, and without it oxidant stress denatures hemoglobin into Heinz bodies and damages the membrane, causing episodes of intravascular and extravascular hemolysis.

points: Folate (as methylene-THF) donates the carbon for thymidylate synthase to turn dUMP into dTMP, so deficiency stalls DNA synthesis and gives megaloblasts.
Methionine synthase uses B12 to move a methyl from methyl-THF to homocysteine, making methionine and freeing THF.
In B12 deficiency folate gets trapped as methyl-THF, so DNA synthesis stalls the same way.
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase needs B12 to turn methylmalonyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA.
B12 deficiency: high homocysteine and high methylmalonic acid, with possible subacute combined degeneration of dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts.
Folate deficiency: high homocysteine with normal methylmalonic acid and no neurologic signs.
notes.why: Both vitamins feed one-carbon metabolism, and the shared step is the supply of methylene-THF for thymidylate synthase. Without enough dTMP, DNA replication stalls while RNA and protein synthesis continue, so nuclear maturation lags behind the cytoplasm and precursors become megaloblasts, many of which die in the marrow. In B12 deficiency, methionine synthase cannot remove the methyl group from methyl-THF, so folate is trapped in a form the cell cannot use (the folate trap) and homocysteine rises in both deficiencies. Only methylmalonyl-CoA mutase needs B12 and not folate, so methylmalonic acid rises in B12 deficiency alone, and only B12 deficiency causes the neurologic disease.

points: Vitamin K is the cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase in the liver, which adds a carboxyl to glutamate residues on factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S.
The resulting gamma-carboxyglutamate residues bind calcium, which bridges them to phosphatidylserine exposed on activated platelets, placing clotting complexes on the platelet surface.
Vitamin K epoxide reductase recycles vitamin K and is the enzyme warfarin blocks.
Deficiency (newborns, fat malabsorption, long antibiotic courses) prolongs the PT first because factor VII has the shortest half-life.
notes.why: Gamma-glutamyl carboxylase adds a second carboxyl group to specific glutamate residues, making gamma-carboxyglutamate (Gla), whose paired negative charges bind calcium. Calcium then bridges Gla domains to negatively charged phosphatidylserine on activated platelets, concentrating clotting complexes at the injury, which is why calcium-chelating citrate and EDTA stop blood from clotting in a tube. Each carboxylation oxidizes vitamin K to its epoxide, and vitamin K epoxide reductase regenerates it; warfarin blocks this enzyme, so factor VII, with the shortest half-life, falls first and the PT prolongs early. Protein C also has a short half-life, which explains the brief hypercoagulable window and warfarin skin necrosis when therapy starts without heparin.

summary: The genetics behind inherited blood diseases and blood cancers: the sickle mutation, thalassemia gene counts, inheritance patterns, driver mutations and translocations, Fanconi anemia, and inherited clotting risk. Exam questions ask you to predict how sickling changes, how many alpha genes are missing, what a child's risk is, and which gene a translocation turns on or off.

points: A single base change in the beta globin gene (chromosome 11) swaps glutamate for valine at position 6.
Valine is hydrophobic; in deoxygenated HbS it sticks into a pocket on a neighboring hemoglobin, and the molecules polymerize into long fibers.
Polymers bend the cell into a rigid sickle, which blocks small vessels and is destroyed early (hemolysis).
More sickling: hypoxia, acidosis (right shift increases deoxyhemoglobin), dehydration (higher hemoglobin concentration), infection, and cold.
Less sickling: high HbF, which does not join the polymer; this is why infants are protected for the first months of life.
Sickle trait (HbAS) is usually silent but can cause hematuria and loss of urine concentrating ability from sickling in the hypoxic, hypertonic renal medulla.
notes.why: Valine at position 6 creates a hydrophobic patch on the surface of beta globin, and in the deoxy conformation that patch fits a hydrophobic pocket on a neighboring tetramer, so deoxy HbS molecules stack into long fibers. Polymer formation depends steeply on how much HbS is deoxygenated and how concentrated it is, so hypoxia, acidosis (through the Bohr effect), and dehydration promote sickling, while HbF, which cannot join the polymer, dilutes it. Rigid, adhesive sickled cells block small vessels and are cleared early. In sickle trait each cell has less than half HbS, so sickling needs an extreme setting such as the hypoxic, hypertonic, acidic renal medulla.

points: Alpha globin: four genes, two on each chromosome 16; alpha thalassemia is usually caused by gene deletions.

One gene deleted: silent carrier. Two: alpha thalassemia trait with mild microcytosis. Three: HbH disease (beta4 tetramers) with moderate hemolytic anemia. Four: Hb Barts (gamma4) with hydrops fetalis.
Hb Barts and HbH bind O2 so tightly that they deliver almost none.
Two deletions on the same chromosome (cis) can pass a zero-gene chromosome to a child; this pattern is more common in people of Southeast Asian ancestry.
Beta thalassemia is usually caused by point mutations (splice site, promoter, nonsense), giving reduced (beta+) or absent (beta0) beta chains.

Beta thalassemia minor: mild microcytosis with HbA2 above about 3.5%. Major: severe anemia after about 6 months as HbF falls, with excess alpha chains precipitating in precursors (ineffective erythropoiesis).
notes.why: Thalassemia is a problem of chain imbalance as much as a shortage of hemoglobin. Because four genes encode alpha globin, severity steps up with each deletion, and when alpha chains are scarce the unpaired gamma chains (fetus) or beta chains (after birth) form Hb Barts and HbH, tetramers with very high oxygen affinity and no cooperativity that deliver little oxygen. In beta thalassemia, mostly from point mutations that impair transcription, splicing, or translation, unpaired alpha chains are insoluble and precipitate in erythroid precursors, killing them in the marrow. Beta thalassemia major appears after about 6 months because gamma chains pair with alpha chains until the switch to beta chain production.

points: X-linked recessive: hemophilia A (factor VIII), hemophilia B (factor IX), G6PD deficiency. Carrier mother: each son 50% affected, each daughter 50% carrier. Affected father: all daughters carriers, no sons affected.
Autosomal recessive: sickle cell disease and the thalassemias. Two carrier parents: 25% affected, 50% carriers, 25% unaffected noncarriers.
Autosomal dominant: most hereditary spherocytosis (ankyrin, spectrin, band 3) and most von Willebrand disease. One affected parent: 50% of children affected.
notes.why: The hemophilia A, hemophilia B, and G6PD genes lie on the X chromosome, so a male with one mutant copy is affected, a female is usually a carrier, and an affected father passes his X to every daughter and his Y to every son. Sickle cell disease and the thalassemias are autosomal recessive because one normal globin gene makes enough functional chains for nearly normal red cells. Hereditary spherocytosis and most von Willebrand disease are autosomal dominant because half the normal amount of a structural or multimeric protein is not enough, or the mutant protein interferes with the normal one.

points: CML: t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome joins BCR on chromosome 22 to ABL1 from chromosome 9.
BCR-ABL1 is a tyrosine kinase that is always on, driving proliferation and blocking apoptosis; imatinib blocks its ATP-binding site.
Polycythemia vera: JAK2 V617F (valine to phenylalanine) disables the inhibitory pseudokinase region of JAK2.
JAK2 then signals through STAT without erythropoietin, so red cells (and often granulocytes and platelets) expand while erythropoietin is low.
notes.why: Tyrosine kinases normally signal only when a growth factor binds, which keeps cell production matched to demand. In CML the BCR portion of the fusion protein makes ABL1 oligomerize, so the kinase is always on and drives proliferation without growth factor, and because the fusion arises in a stem cell, granulocytes at every stage expand, often with basophilia. JAK2 V617F disables the inhibitory pseudokinase domain, so JAK2 attached to the erythropoietin, thrombopoietin, and G-CSF receptors signals without ligand. Red cell mass rises while normal feedback suppresses erythropoietin, which separates polycythemia vera from secondary polycythemia.

points: Many lymphoma translocations involve chromosome 14 because it carries the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus, whose strong enhancer drives the partner gene in B cells.
t(8;14) Burkitt lymphoma: MYC overexpressed, driving very rapid proliferation (starry sky pattern).
t(14;18) follicular lymphoma: BCL2 overexpressed, blocking apoptosis, so cells accumulate slowly.
t(11;14) mantle cell lymphoma: cyclin D1 overexpressed, pushing cells from G1 into S phase.
t(15;17) acute promyelocytic leukemia: PML-RARA fusion blocks differentiation at the promyelocyte stage; all-trans retinoic acid releases the block.
notes.why: Translocations cause cancer in two ways: by placing an intact gene under a strong foreign enhancer, or by fusing two genes into a new protein. In B cells the immunoglobulin heavy chain enhancer on chromosome 14 is highly active, so MYC, BCL2, or cyclin D1 moved next to it is overexpressed, and the gene involved predicts behavior: MYC drives rapid proliferation (Burkitt), BCL2 blocks apoptosis so cells pile up slowly (follicular), and cyclin D1 pushes cells past the G1 checkpoint (mantle cell). In acute promyelocytic leukemia, PML-RARA represses the retinoic acid target genes needed for differentiation, so high-dose all-trans retinoic acid overcomes the block and lets promyelocytes mature.

points: Mostly autosomal recessive defects in Fanconi pathway genes that repair DNA interstrand crosslinks.
Cells break chromosomes when exposed to crosslinking agents (diepoxybutane or mitomycin C test).
Progressive marrow failure in childhood, short stature, absent or small thumbs and radial anomalies, and cafe-au-lait spots.
High risk of myelodysplastic syndrome, AML, and squamous cell carcinomas.
notes.why: Interstrand crosslinks tie both DNA strands together and stop replication; the Fanconi pathway recognizes replication forks stalled at crosslinks and coordinates their repair with homologous recombination proteins, including BRCA2 (FANCD1). Without it, crosslinks from normal metabolism such as reactive aldehydes accumulate, and hematopoietic stem cells are progressively lost, causing marrow failure. The same genomic instability explains chromosome breakage with diepoxybutane or mitomycin C, the high risk of AML and squamous cell cancers, and the developmental defects of the thumb, radius, and growth.

points: Factor V Leiden: a point mutation at the activated protein C cleavage site makes factor Va resistant to inactivation, so thrombin generation runs longer.
It is the most common inherited thrombophilia in people of European ancestry.
Prothrombin G20210A: a change in the untranslated region raises prothrombin levels, so more thrombin can form.
Both raise venous thrombosis risk several-fold, and risk multiplies with estrogen, pregnancy, or surgery; PT and PTT are normal.
notes.why: Activated protein C normally stops thrombin generation by cleaving factor Va at specific arginine residues, beginning with arginine 506. Factor V Leiden replaces that arginine with glutamine, so Va is inactivated much more slowly and the prothrombinase complex keeps making thrombin. The prothrombin G20210A variant sits in the 3' untranslated region and raises the amount of prothrombin mRNA, so plasma prothrombin is higher and more thrombin can form at each injury. Both add procoagulant activity, so the PT and PTT, which detect factor deficiencies, stay normal, and diagnosis needs an activated protein C resistance assay or genetic testing.

tricks.text: When a B cell lymphoma translocation includes chromosome 14, the immunoglobulin heavy chain enhancer is turning on the partner gene: MYC on 8, cyclin D1 on 11, BCL2 on 18.

tricks.label: Sickling follows anything that adds deoxyhemoglobin or concentrates it
tricks.text: Hypoxia and acidosis increase deoxyhemoglobin; dehydration packs hemoglobin closer together. HbF dilutes HbS and cannot polymerize with it.

highYield: Glutamate to valine at beta globin position 6 makes deoxygenated HbS polymerize.
Sickle cell crises tend to begin after about 6 months of age as HbF falls.
HbA2 above about 3.5% supports beta thalassemia minor.
Hydrops fetalis in a fetus of two parents with alpha thalassemia trait means all four alpha genes are deleted.
BCR-ABL1 from t(9;22) is the target of tyrosine kinase inhibitors in CML.
Low erythropoietin with high red cell mass points to JAK2-driven polycythemia vera.
Short stature, absent thumbs, and pancytopenia in a child suggest Fanconi anemia.
Venous thrombosis on oral contraceptives with resistance to activated protein C suggests factor V Leiden.
pitfalls: Alpha thalassemia usually comes from deletions; beta thalassemia usually comes from point mutations.
BCL2 blocks apoptosis (follicular lymphoma), while MYC drives proliferation (Burkitt lymphoma).
Factor V Leiden is a defect in factor V itself; protein C deficiency is a shortage of the brake.
All daughters of a father with hemophilia are carriers, and none of his sons are affected because sons get his Y chromosome.
Fanconi anemia (DNA crosslink repair, pancytopenia) is distinct from Diamond-Blackfan anemia (ribosomal protein genes, pure red cell aplasia), though both can involve the thumbs.

summary: Immune reactions that target blood: autoimmune hemolysis, transfusion reactions, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, antiphospholipid syndrome, Epstein-Barr virus in B cells, and infection risk after loss of the spleen. Exam questions ask you to classify a reaction by hypersensitivity type, read a Coombs test, sort transfusion reactions by timing, and explain why some antibodies cause clots instead of bleeding.

points: Warm type: IgG binds red cells best at body temperature, 37 °C (98.6 °F).
Splenic macrophages with Fc receptors nibble IgG-coated membrane, leaving spherocytes, and hemolysis is extravascular.
Warm causes: idiopathic, SLE, CLL, and some drugs.
Cold agglutinin type: IgM binds red cells at temperatures below about 30 °C (86 °F), as in cool fingers, toes, ears, and nose, and fixes complement.
Cold findings: red cell clumping on the smear, acrocyanosis in the cold, and hemolysis driven by complement (C3b removal in the liver and some intravascular lysis).
Cold causes: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, EBV infectious mononucleosis, and lymphoproliferative disorders.
Direct Coombs test: anti-human globulin added to the patient's red cells clumps them if IgG or complement is already on their surface; warm is usually IgG positive, cold is usually C3 positive only.
Indirect Coombs test looks for free antibodies in serum, as in prenatal antibody screening and crossmatching.
notes.why: Temperature decides which antibody class binds and which effector destroys the cell. Warm IgG binds at 37 °C (98.6 °F) and activates complement less well, so splenic macrophages with Fc gamma receptors remove pieces of coated membrane, the cell reseals as a spherocyte, and hemolysis is extravascular. Cold IgM binds in cool peripheral blood and, as a pentamer, fixes complement efficiently; when the blood rewarms the IgM lets go but C3b stays on the cell, so liver macrophages clear C3b-coated cells and some are lysed by the membrane attack complex. The direct Coombs test detects whatever remains bound: IgG in warm disease, C3 alone in cold agglutinin disease.

points: Type II (antibody against a cell surface antigen): acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, hemolytic disease of the newborn, immune thrombocytopenia.
In hemolytic disease of the newborn, maternal IgG (classically anti-D) crosses the placenta and coats fetal red cells.
Type III (immune complexes deposit and fix complement): cryoglobulinemia, where immunoglobulins that precipitate in the cold form complexes that inflame small vessels.
Mixed cryoglobulinemia is strongly linked to hepatitis C and causes palpable purpura, joint pain, glomerulonephritis, and low complement.
Immediate (type I-like) reactions: allergic and anaphylactic transfusion reactions.
notes.why: The hypersensitivity type is set by where the antibody meets its antigen. In type II reactions the antigen sits on a cell, so antibody tags that cell for complement lysis or phagocytosis, which is why transfusion reactions, autoimmune hemolysis, and hemolytic disease of the newborn all destroy the targeted red cells. In type III reactions the antibody meets a soluble antigen, and the immune complexes lodge in vessel walls and glomeruli, where they activate complement and recruit neutrophils; in cryoglobulinemia these complexes precipitate in the cold and cause purpura, glomerulonephritis, and low complement.

points: Heparin binds platelet factor 4 (released from platelet alpha granules) and forms a new antigen.
IgG binds the heparin and PF4 complex, and its Fc portion engages Fc receptors on platelets, activating them.
Activated platelets aggregate, release more PF4, and shed procoagulant particles, while antibody-coated platelets are cleared.
The platelet count falls by more than half about 5 to 10 days after starting heparin (sooner with recent heparin exposure).
The danger is clotting: venous and arterial thrombosis, with bleeding uncommon; risk is higher with unfractionated heparin.
notes.why: Platelet factor 4 is a positively charged protein from alpha granules, and heparin, a long negatively charged chain, binds several PF4 molecules and changes their shape, creating a new epitope. IgG against this complex forms immune complexes on the platelet surface whose Fc portions cross-link platelet Fc gamma RIIa receptors, activating platelets and releasing more PF4 in a self-amplifying loop. Activated platelets and monocytes generate thrombin, so the patient clots while platelets are consumed and cleared. The 5 to 10 day delay reflects the time needed to make IgG, and onset is sooner when antibody already exists from recent exposure.

points: Antibodies target phospholipid-binding proteins: lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta2 glycoprotein I.
In the test tube, lupus anticoagulant interferes with the phospholipid-dependent steps of the PTT, so the PTT is prolonged and does not correct with mixing.
In the body, the antibodies activate endothelium, platelets, monocytes, and complement, causing venous and arterial thrombosis.
Placental thrombosis leads to recurrent pregnancy loss and preeclampsia.
Anticardiolipin can give a false-positive syphilis screen; the syndrome can be primary or occur with SLE.
notes.why: Phospholipid-dependent clotting tests supply only a little phospholipid as the surface for clotting complexes, and lupus anticoagulant antibodies bound to beta2 glycoprotein I or prothrombin on that phospholipid compete with the complexes, so the PTT is prolonged and does not correct with mixing. In the body, phospholipid surfaces are plentiful, and the same antibodies instead activate endothelial cells, platelets, monocytes, and complement and increase tissue factor expression. The net effect is thrombosis in any vascular bed, and in the placenta it causes infarction and poor placentation, leading to pregnancy loss and preeclampsia.

points: EBV glycoprotein gp350 binds CD21 (complement receptor 2) on B cells, and the virus stays latent in memory B cells.
CD8 cytotoxic T cells expand to kill infected B cells; these are the atypical lymphocytes of mononucleosis.
Mononucleosis: fever, pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and positive heterophile antibody.
Latent EBV proteins drive B cell growth; when T cell control fails or cofactors act, lymphoma can follow.
EBV-linked cancers: endemic Burkitt lymphoma (with malaria as cofactor), Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphomas after transplant or in HIV, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
notes.why: EBV gp350 binds CD21 (complement receptor 2) on B cells, and latent viral proteins such as EBNA2 and LMP1, which mimics an active CD40 receptor, drive the infected B cells to proliferate. A strong CD8 T cell response controls these B cells; the activated T cells are the atypical lymphocytes, and lymphoid hyperplasia enlarges nodes, tonsils, and spleen. The virus then persists in memory B cells for life, so when T cell surveillance weakens (transplant, HIV) or a cofactor such as endemic malaria is present, the viral growth program can contribute to lymphoma.

points: Polysaccharide capsules resist phagocytosis unless the bacteria are coated with antibody or complement.
The spleen filters blood, its marginal zone B cells make fast IgM against capsules, and its macrophages clear opsonized bacteria.

Without a spleen (surgical removal or sickle cell autosplenectomy from repeated infarcts), sepsis from Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Neisseria meningitidis can be rapid and fatal.
Smear clues of asplenia: Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells, and thrombocytosis.
Conjugate vaccines link the capsule sugar to a protein, recruit T cell help, and give class-switched IgG and memory, even in infants.
notes.why: A polysaccharide capsule blocks complement deposition and hides surface ligands, so these bacteria are cleared mainly after opsonization by antibody and complement and capture by fixed macrophages. The spleen is suited to this because blood percolates slowly through its cords past macrophages, and its marginal zone B cells make rapid IgM against polysaccharides without T cell help. Without a spleen, poorly opsonized bacteria multiply in the blood and cause overwhelming sepsis. Plain polysaccharide is a T-independent antigen that gives weak responses in young children, so conjugating it to a protein recruits helper T cells, class switching, and memory.

tricks.label: Warm is G, cold is M
tricks.text: Warm autoimmune hemolysis uses IgG and makes spherocytes in the spleen. Cold agglutinin disease uses IgM, which clumps cells in cold fingers and brings complement.

tricks.label: SHiNE SKiS
tricks.text: Encapsulated organisms: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, Neisseria meningitidis, Escherichia coli, Salmonella, Klebsiella pneumoniae, group B Streptococcus.

tricks.label: Some antibodies clot instead of bleed
tricks.text: HIT and antiphospholipid syndrome both lower platelets or prolong a lab test, yet both cause thrombosis because the antibodies activate platelets or endothelium.

highYield: Spherocytes with a positive direct Coombs test for IgG in a patient with SLE or CLL means warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
Hemolysis after Mycoplasma pneumonia with a C3-positive Coombs test fits cold agglutinin disease.
Fever, flank pain, and red urine minutes into a transfusion means an acute hemolytic reaction from ABO mismatch.
Anaphylaxis without fever during a first transfusion suggests IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies.
Respiratory distress with bilateral infiltrates within 6 hours of transfusion, without volume overload, means TRALI.
A platelet count falling by half a week into heparin therapy with a new clot means HIT.
Recurrent miscarriage plus a prolonged PTT that does not correct with mixing suggests antiphospholipid syndrome.
Howell-Jolly bodies on a smear mean absent or nonfunctioning spleen.
pitfalls: HIT causes clots; bleeding is uncommon even though platelets are low.
Lupus anticoagulant prolongs the PTT in the lab and causes thrombosis in the patient.
Atypical lymphocytes in mononucleosis are reactive CD8 T cells; EBV itself infects B cells.
Febrile nonhemolytic reactions have fever without hemolysis; anaphylactic reactions have hypotension and wheeze without fever.
Cryoglobulinemia is type III (immune complex), while autoimmune hemolysis is type II.
